title: Hard exam 5
about: Ten single-choice questions with traps: signals that only reach the foreground, status of pipelines, alternations without `-E`, units without a letter, aliases that children do not inherit and scripts you can execute but not read.

questions.title: Ctrl+C at an empty prompt
questions.text: You run `sleep 100 &` and then, at the empty prompt, press Ctrl+C. What does `jobs` show afterwards?

options.t: Nothing: Ctrl+C terminated the job.
options.why: Ctrl+C is sent to the foreground; the background job is not affected.

options.t: The job as stopped, as if you had pressed Ctrl+Z.
options.why: Nothing suspended it either.

options.t: The job still running.
options.why: The keyboard signals go only to the foreground process, and at an empty prompt there is none, so `sleep` carries on.

options.t: The job as done, because Ctrl+C makes the shell wait for it.
options.why: Ctrl+C does not make the shell wait for anything.

questions.title: Two words in a read
questions.text: What does `echo "one two three" | { read a b; echo "$a|$b"; }` print?

options.t: `one|two`
options.why: The last variable of `read` receives the whole remaining text, not just one word.

options.t: `one two three|`
options.why: The first variable takes only the first word.

options.t: `one|two three`
options.why: `read` splits the line into fields and gives the rest of the line to the last variable.

options.t: It waits for the user to type, because `read` always reads from the keyboard.
options.why: `read` reads from stdin, which here is the pipe.

questions.title: Status of a pipeline and of a subshell
questions.text: What do `false | true; echo $?` and `(exit 3); echo $?` print?

options.why: The status of a pipeline is that of its last command, and `exit 3` ends the subshell with status 3.
`true` is the last command of the pipeline; the subshell exits with 3 and `$?` reports it.
`exit` inside the parentheses ends only the subshell, but its status is not lost.
`false` is not the last command, so its status does not count.

questions.title: Alternatives in a recursive search
questions.text: A student wants the lines that contain `foo` or `bar` in all the files below `dir`, and types `grep -r 'foo|bar' dir`. It prints nothing although `dir/f1` contains `foo here`. What is wrong?

options.t: `-r` needs the name of the directory to end with a slash, as in `dir/`.
options.why: It works without it.

options.t: Patterns can only be read from a pattern file that is given with the option `-f`.
options.why: A pattern on the command line is fine.

options.t: `-r` cannot be combined with a regular expression, only with fixed words.
options.why: It searches the files below the directory using the same patterns.

options.t: A basic regular expression treats `|` as plain text; `-E` is needed.
options.why: Without `-E`, `foo|bar` is the literal text `foo|bar`, which appears nowhere.

questions.title: Two steps up and one down
questions.text: Linux has a single directory tree. Starting in any directory, you run `cd /usr/local/bin`, then `cd ../../lib`, then `cd ..`, and `pwd`. What is printed?

options.t: `/usr/local`
options.why: The second `cd` goes up two levels, to `/usr`, and then into `lib`; the last `cd ..` goes up once more.

options.t: `/usr`
options.why: `../../lib` from `/usr/local/bin` is `/usr/lib`; the last `cd ..` goes back to `/usr`.
`/` is the root: `/usr` is one level below it, which is where the last `cd ..` ends.

options.t: `/usr/lib`
options.why: The last `cd ..` leaves `/usr/lib`.

questions.title: Size without a unit
questions.text: A student wants the files larger than 1000 bytes and types `find . -size +1000`. A file of 2000 bytes is not listed, but one of 600000 bytes is. What is wrong?

options.t: `+` selects the smaller files, so the two signs have been swapped by mistake.
options.why: `+` means larger than.

options.t: With no letter the unit is a 512-byte block; it needs `+1000c`.
options.why: `+1000` means more than 1000 blocks, about half a megabyte.

options.t: `-size` is a test that works only with directories, not with regular files.
options.why: It works on any file.

options.t: The test needs a file name as well, for example `-name '*'`, in order to work.
options.why: Tests combine freely; no name is required.

questions.title: What the shell does
questions.text: Which statement about the shell is TRUE?

options.t: `cd` is an external program, `/bin/cd`, which the shell starts in a child process.
options.why: `cd` is a builtin: it has to change the directory of the shell itself.

options.t: `powershell.exe` is one of the usual shells of the Unix-like systems such as Linux.
options.why: It belongs to Microsoft Windows.

options.t: It starts an external command as a new process and, without `&`, waits for it.
options.why: Read, parse, run, wait and show the prompt: that is the cycle of the shell.

options.t: The shell is the graphical interface that sits between the user and the kernel of the system.
options.why: It is a text interface.

questions.title: Users and groups in sequence
questions.text: On a Debian-like system, the group `dev` is created with `addgroup dev` and gets GID 1005. Then root runs `adduser ana dev`, `adduser luis dev` and `deluser ana dev`. What does `grep '^dev:' /etc/group` print?

options.t: `dev:x:1005:ana,luis`
options.why: `deluser ana dev` took ana out of the group again.
Only ana was removed; luis is still a member.

options.t: `dev:x:1005:luis`
options.why: `adduser user group` adds a member and `deluser user group` removes one, editing the last field of the line.

options.t: Nothing, because `deluser` removes the group when a member is taken out.
options.why: With two arguments `deluser` only removes the user from the group.

questions.title: Executable but unreadable
questions.text: `ana` owns the script `s.sh` (a correct bash script) with mode `--x------`. She runs `./s.sh` and then `bash s.sh`. What happens?

options.t: Both work, because she is the owner and has `x`.
options.why: To run a script, the interpreter has to read it.

options.t: `./s.sh` works and `bash s.sh` fails, because only the second one needs to read the file.
options.why: `./s.sh` needs to read the file as well: the shell opens it to run its commands.

options.t: `./s.sh` fails, but `bash s.sh` works, because `bash` does not need the `x` bit.
options.why: `bash s.sh` needs `r`, which is missing too.

options.t: Both fail with `Permission denied`.
options.why: A script needs `r` to be read, and `./` also needs `x`; the file only has `x`.

questions.title: Aliases and child shells
questions.text: At her prompt, ana defines `alias ll='ls -l'`. Then she runs `bash -c ll`. What happens?

options.t: It lists the current directory in long format.
options.why: The alias exists only in the shell where it was typed.

options.t: It fails with "ll: command not found".
options.why: The new bash is a child process and it does not inherit the aliases of its parent.

options.t: It prints the text `ls -l`.
options.why: Aliases are expanded, not printed; and none exists in the child.

options.t: It works only if `ll` had been exported with `export ll`.
options.why: `export` applies to variables and functions, not to aliases.
